How much should you keep in the bank after 65? Your account feels like a box with one key, but in law seven hands can reach into it. We go through each one on its own government page, with an invented couple, Hal and Rita ($3,700 a month of Social Security landing in one checking account that holds $86,000), and Rita's sister Joan.

THE SEVEN HANDS (illustration, Nov 2026)
• SSA: only if you get SSI. Savings limit $2,000 for one person, $3,000 for a couple. Giving it away can cost up to 36 months.
• Your state: Medicare Savings Programs. QMB 2026: income $1,350, savings $9,950. Joan is $2,050 over, which costs her $2,434.80 a year. Some states allow more, so apply anyway.
• IRS: there is no checking-account limit. Banks report CASH over $10,000, and splitting deposits to dodge that report (structuring) is the crime. The IRS does see interest ($10 or more means a 1099-INT).
• Your bank: setoff can take a loan payment from your account. A credit card can't be paid from your deposits unless you agreed to autopay. A brokerage can pause a suspicious withdrawal for up to 15 business days and call your trusted contact.
• A creditor: on a garnishment order, the bank must protect the Social Security deposited in the last two months, automatically. For Hal and Rita that's $7,400; $78,600 is exposed. Federal-debt and child-support orders are the exception.
• State treasurer: a dormant account is turned over to the state. Log in once a year.
• FDIC: $250,000 per person, per bank, per ownership category. After a death, six months, then recalculated. Name beneficiaries.
THE NUMBER: keep about two months of benefits where Social Security lands, and move the rest to a bank where you owe nothing. At the national 12-month CD average that's +$1,328 a year for Hal and Rita.

Congress just passed a Social Security bill, the Claiming Age Clarity Act (H.R. 5284). We read the whole thing on screen: one page, no dollar amounts. It renames three ages and changes no benefit. But there are five names you'll hear about Social Security this year, and one of them, a proposal, would change the size of your check. An invented couple, Ron (62 next year) and Debbie, shows the number behind each name.

THE NAME · THE NUMBER (illustration, today's dollars)
• Minimum (62, was "early eligibility age"): still 70% of your benefit. Ron: $1,680.
• Standard (67, was "full" and "normal retirement age"): still 100%. Ron: $2,400.
• Maximum (70): "delayed retirement credit" goes as a term; the 8% a year stays. Ron: $2,976. Break-even 62 vs 70 ≈ age 80 and 4 months. Raises are a percentage, so inflation doesn't move it.
• The word the research never tested: "monthly". 70 pays the biggest monthly check, not always the biggest lifetime total. For a couple, the widow's check decides it: Debbie $1,980 vs $2,976, +$996 a month.
• Claimed early and regret it? You can withdraw within 12 months and repay.
• Insolvent (late 2032): not zero. 78% of scheduled benefits are still payable if Congress does nothing.
• Flat (a proposal, not a bill): one dollar raise for everyone, set by the 20th-percentile check. 2026: $34.20 instead of $57.90 for the average retiree; 80% get less; the smallest checks gain. It closes about half the 75-year gap but delays the trust funds' run-out by only two years. It also shrinks the reward for waiting: at 90, Ron's gap falls from $1,296 to about $798.

There's a new bill in Congress — the Blue Collar Social Security Fairness Act, announced September 24, 2026 by Rep. THE PUNCH CARD — the bill's two ways in
• PATH 1 — 20 qualifying years (one "base point" per year; a year counts only with 8+ months of the work in it).
• PATH 2 — 15 weighted points: ages 18–34 earn ½ point a year · 35–44 one point · 45–54 one and a half · 55+ two points.
• The catches: the official occupation list doesn't exist yet (SSA + Labor + HHS get a year to write it); you still need 40 lifetime work credits; and page five sets a covered worker's earnings-test limit at $833.33⅓ a month — about $10,000 a year, less than half the standard $24,480. This check is for workers who are done working.
• Don't confuse it with the Social Security Fairness Act signed into law in January 2025 (the WEP/GPO repeal) — that one is real money some retirees can claim today.
